title: Why selected, why deferred: forcing in and out

blocks.text: 9.3.2 Why Selected, Why Deferred: Forcing In and Out

Two emails reach GridCap's optimization team on the morning the base plan is published. The Ridge region manager writes: "P024, the undergrounding job we promised Ridge customers, is not in the plan. Why?" And a finance analyst writes: "P032 costs $5,680k in one year. Why is it in?" Lesson 9.3.1 gave part of an answer: as the plan stands, every budget row is too full to take P024. But the solver is not bound to the plan as it stands. It could drop one project, move two, and fit P024. The real question is what that would cost, and what would give way.

This lesson answers it the way an optimizer can prove: **force the opposite decision and re-solve**. Force P024 in, and the drop in NPV is the price of P024; force P032 out, and the drop is what P032 is worth to the plan. The comparison of the two plans then says which projects give way, and the rows of lesson 9.3.1 say which rule makes them. Such a re-solve is often called a **counterfactual**: the best plan in a world where one decision went the other way.
GridCap is a fictional utility, generated for this course; no number in it describes a real one.

In this lesson, a project is **selected** when it is in the plan, and **deferred** when it is not: utilities say deferred because a candidate left out of this cycle's plan comes back in the next cycle's list. A selected project that starts after its earliest allowed year is **late**; lesson 7.1.4 counted nine of them.
The Model
The model of lesson 9.3.1, whole, with this lesson's three forcing rows marked. A forcing row replaces the project's once row; a forced-in must-do keeps its must row.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years project $`i`$ may use; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$ years. For one re-solve: $`F^{+} \subseteq P`$ the projects forced in, $`F^{-} \subseteq P`$ those forced out, and $`A \subseteq \{(i,t) : i \in F^{+},\ t \in T_i\}`$ the forced-in projects pinned to a start year.
**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$, with $`\text{started}(i) = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$ and $`\text{by}(i, t) = \sum_{s \in T_i,\, s \le t} x_{i,s}`$.
**Objective.**
z = \max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus (M \cup F^{+} \cup F^{-}) && \text{(once}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\text{started}(i) &= 1 && \forall i \in F^{+} \setminus M && \text{(in}_i) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
\text{started}(i) &= 0 && \forall i \in F^{-} && \text{(out}_i) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall (i,t) \in A && \text{(in}_{i,t}) \quad \leftarrow \text{this lesson} \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in g} \text{started}(i) &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\text{by}(c, t) &\le \text{by}(p(c),\, t - L_c) && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\textstyle\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}
With $`z^*`$ the best NPV of the base model and $`z^*_{\text{in}(i)}`$, $`z^*_{\text{out}(i)}`$, $`z^*_{\text{at}(i,t)}`$ the best NPV with one forcing added, the **cost of a decision** is
Each is $`\ge 0`$: a forcing row only removes plans, so the best plan that is left can be no better than the best plan overall. When a forced model has no feasible plan at all, the cost is undefined.
The Cost of a Decision Is What the Best Plan Loses When You Force the Opposite
`why.force` reverses one decision of the base plan and re-solves. A project in the plan is forced out, a project out of it is forced in, and a year, if given, pins the start:

The forcing is a change to the scenario, not an edit of the solved model: `build` writes the model again from the scenario, with the `in_` or `out_` row in place of the project's once row. Each re-solve runs to a proven optimum (relative gap 0), because a cost is the difference of two optima; with a gap tolerance, the difference could be the solver stopping early rather than the decision. `force_one.py` answers the two emails:

base: NPV $24,260k, 27 funded

force P024 in: OPTIMAL, NPV $23,987k, cost $273k (its own NPV at its best start: $490k)
  added ['P024', 'P037']  dropped ['P005', 'P009', 'P016']
  moved ['P008 2031->2029', 'P011 2031->2029', 'P018 2030->2031']

P024 is deferred because funding it costs the portfolio $273k of NPV, the same $273k lesson 7.1.3 found when a planner forced it in at Post-Opt (the base scenario there also had region floors, which did not change this plan). P032 is selected because the best plan without it is worth $112k less.

Neither number is the project's own NPV, and the second shows how far apart they can be. P032 brings $3,678k of NPV, yet losing it costs only $112k, because its $5,680k of 2027 money does not vanish: the re-solve spends it on P002, P036, P037 and P038 and rearranges eight start years. What a project is worth to a plan is its NPV less the NPV of the best use of its money and its place in the rules. Only a re-solve measures that. A ranking by NPV, or by NPV per dollar, cannot (lesson 7.1.4 found the same for ratios).
A Forced Re-Solve Says What Gives Way, and the Rules Say Why
A cost tells a planner how much; the reason is in the rows. Two sources give it, and a good answer uses both:

items: **The rows that refuse the project as the plan stands** (lesson 9.3.1's refusals), turned into facts: for a budget row, the room left and the least the project needs there; for an alternative row, the option already funded. `why.rules_against` writes them.
**What gives way in the forced plan**: the projects dropped, added and moved. That is the cheapest way the solver found to make room, so it names the projects the deferred one is competing with.

Put together, the answers read as sentences a planner can check:

items: **P024** spends $850k a year for two years, and no year of its window has more than $150k left. To fit it, the best plan drops P005, P009 and P016, adds P037 and moves three projects, and ends $273k lower.

**P002** is the repair option for asset A001, whose replacement P001 is funded, and `alt_G001` allows one of the two; the money is short as well. Forcing P002 in drops P001, as the alternative row says it must, and the plan ends $112k lower.

blocks.text: The order matters: the rule first, then what gives way, then the cost. A cost with no rule ("it would cost $273k") invites the reply "then cut something else"; the rule shows that every year is full, and the forced plan shows what "something else" would be.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Forcing the Rules Cannot Satisfy Is Answered by a Rule, Not a Price
Some reversals have no price because no plan allows them. Force a must-do out:

force P017 out: INFEASIBLE; its rows ['must_P017', 'out_P017']
force P039 out: INFEASIBLE; its rows ['must_P039', 'out_P039']

The forced model holds both $`\text{started}(i) = 1`$ (must) and $`\text{started}(i) = 0`$ (out), and no plan keeps both. The answer to "why is P017 selected?" is then the rule, "it is a must-do", and the cost is not "very large" but undefined. A report must say "infeasible: must_P017", never print a number.

Here the conflict is plain from the project's own rows. When it is not (a project forced in whose parent cannot fit, or a forced-in pair that two budgets cannot both carry), the conflicting rows are found with the tools of lesson 9.1.3 (an IIS) and worded with those of lesson 9.1.6. Some study guides say that an infeasible forced-in solve means the project "violates hard physical or timing constraints". Read it more narrowly: it means the forcing contradicts the model's rules as written, and which rules is a question for an IIS, not a guess.
Report Every Project, and Read Small Costs as Near Ties

Look at how small most costs are against a plan worth $24,260k. Forcing P004 in costs $64k, 0.26% of the NPV; moving P029 a year earlier costs $8k. And many different forcings cost exactly the same. The program groups the forcings whose re-solves return the very same plan:

forcings that land on the same plan:
  cost  112: P002 in, P036 in, P038 in, P001 out, P032 out
  cost   64: P004 in, P037 in, P009 out, P016 out, P020 out
  cost  114: P006 in, P013 in
  cost  113: P027 in, P005 out
  cost  870: P030 in, P028 out
  cost  135: P008 out, P011 out
  cost  121: P021 out, P026 out

Ten different reversals lead to just two plans: one worth $64k less than the best, one worth $112k less. These are the runner-up plans of the portfolio, and the forcings are different doors into them. That is what to tell a planner: P004 is not out because it is a bad project; it is out because a plan with it exists that is only $64k worse, and the solver must pick one. A cost of exactly 0 would mean the forced plan is another optimum, and then "why deferred" has no answer beyond "the solver had to choose" (lesson 10.2.3 covers alternative optima and how to break ties on purpose). On GridCap small no reversal costs 0; the cheapest, P029 a year earlier, costs $8k.

Treat a small cost as a finding in its own right. It says the decision is cheap to override, which is what a planner pushing for P004 wants to know, and it warns that a small change in the inputs could flip the decision, which is what finance wants to know before trusting it.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **The cost of a decision is what the best plan loses when you force the opposite.** Re-solve with $`\text{started}(i) = 1`$ or $`= 0`$ and compare optima. P024 costs $273k to force in; P032 costs $112k to lose, against its own NPV of $3,678k.
**A forced re-solve says what gives way, and the rules say why.** State the rows that refuse the project as the plan stands, then the projects that give way, then the cost.
**A forcing the rules cannot satisfy is answered by a rule, not a price.** Forcing a must-do out is infeasible; report the rows in conflict, never a number.
**Report every project, and read small costs as near ties.** Ten GridCap reversals lead to two runner-up plans, $64k and $112k below the best; a cost of 0 would mean another optimum.

rows: $`\Delta_{\text{in}}(i)`$, what gives way, and the rows that refuse $`i`$
another optimal plan obeys the forcing; the solver chose between ties
a near tie; cheap to override, and sensitive to inputs
the decision is robust; the rows say what makes it so
the forcing breaks a rule; name the rule

blocks.text: **Further reading:** the OR-Tools [MathOpt overview](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (a model built once and solved again unchanged, which is what makes a scenario re-solve cheap to write); the OR-Tools MathOpt sample [`integer_programming.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/samples/python/integer_programming.py) (it reads a plan only after an optimal or feasible termination, the check `solve` makes before a cost is computed); [MathOpt `result.py` (OR-Tools source)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/result.py) (the docstrings of `objective_value` and `best_objective_bound`, the two numbers whose equality a gap of 0 asks for); [Integer Programming, Chapter 9 of Applied Mathematical Programming (MIT 15.053)](https://web.mit.edu/15.053/www/AMP-Chapter-09.pdf) (section 9.1: capital budgeting with go/no-go variables and logical conditions such as one investment only if another, the rules a forcing runs against); L. Challenges

items: Force P024 in *and* P037 out. Predict whether the cost is more or less than $273k, then run it.
P028 and P030 land on the same plan when one is forced out and the other in. Explain why from their windows and costs before you look at the rows.
The report runs 49 re-solves on 40 projects. How many would it run on the medium portfolio, and which projects could you skip without losing an answer?

blocks.text: Design Note: Forcings Are Named Rows, Not Bounds

Lesson 6.5.6 writes a planner's override as bounds on the start variables, which is the lightest way to fix a decision. This lesson writes a forcing as a named row (`in_P024`, `out_P017`) instead. A named row can be reported, diffed between scenarios and named by an IIS when the forcing makes the model infeasible. A bound has no name of its own. Lesson 9.1.3's run showed both ways a bound fails in Gurobi's IIS: a 0-1 variable typed binary never has its bounds in the IIS at all, and one typed integer (as MathOpt's 0-1 variables are when copied to gurobipy) can have them there, but only as a variable's lower or upper bound (25 of them in that IIS), marked exactly as the ordinary 0 and 1 bounds are. Either way, a forcing written as a bound could not be named as the forcing in the very explanation it caused. The cost is one row per forcing, which on a re-solve of one forcing is nothing.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**force_one.py.** Forces P024 in, P032 out and P002 in, prints each cost and what gives way, and forces two must-dos out (*The Cost of a Decision*, *A Forced Re-Solve Says What Gives Way* and *A Forcing the Rules Cannot Satisfy*). *Try:* Force P037 in instead of P024. Predict its cost from the report's first table before you run it.

**why_report.py.** The "why" line for every project: deferred, selected and late, and the forcings that land on the same plan (*Report Every Project*). *Try:* Cut the 2030 budget by $500k in the program's scenario. Predict whether P004 stays the cheapest project to force in.
**why.py.** `force`, `changes` and the rule facts the reports print. It runs nothing itself.
